title: Using Cursor IDE
description: Learn how to use Cursor, an AI-first code editor designed for pair programming with large language models.

data.text: Cursor is a fork of VS Code with AI deeply integrated into the editor. Unlike GitHub Copilot, which functions primarily as an extension, Cursor is built from the ground up to support AI coding workflows. This means the AI has better access to your entire codebase, not just the open file, and it offers richer features for multi-file editing and project generation.

data.title: The main features you will use:
items: Chat — a sidebar panel for conversational coding help with codebase awareness
Composer — a panel for multi-file generation and refactoring from natural language
Inline Edit — select code, press Cmd/Ctrl+K, describe changes, and see them inline
Codebase Indexing — Cursor builds an index of your project for better context-aware suggestions
Terminal Integration — run shell commands through the AI to set up dependencies or run tests

data.text: The Chat panel is where most of your time will be spent. Unlike a generic ChatGPT session, Cursor Chat has access to your open files, your codebase index, and the selected code. You can ask questions like "How does authentication work in this project?" and Cursor will read the relevant files and explain.

data.title: @-mentions give Cursor specific context
data.text: Type @ to mention specific files, folders, or even GitHub issues in your chat. @src/auth.ts limits the context to that file. @docs references your documentation. This dramatically improves the accuracy of responses for large codebases.

Composer is Cursor's most distinctive feature. Open it with Cmd/Ctrl+I and describe what you want to build. Composer will generate code across multiple files, modify existing files, and show you a diff before applying changes. This is ideal for scaffolding new features or refactoring code that spans several files.

data.title: Example Composer prompt
data.content: "Add a new REST endpoint at /api/v1/users/:id/profile that returns the user's profile data with their last 5 activity log entries. Use the existing User and ActivityLog models. Add basic rate limiting. Include input validation."
data.code:
Composer prompt:
"Add a new REST endpoint at `/api/v1/users/:id/profile` that returns the user's profile data with their last 5 activity log entries. Use the existing `User` and `ActivityLog` models. Add basic rate limiting. Include input validation."

data.text: Inline edit (Cmd/Ctrl+K) is the fastest way to make targeted changes. Select a block of code, describe the change, and Cursor rewrites just that block. No need to open a chat or switch panels. Use this for quick refactors, adding comments, renaming variables, or converting syntax.

Cursor builds a local index of your project so it can understand how files relate to each other. This means when you ask "Where is the payment processing logic?", Cursor can actually find it and explain it, rather than guessing. You can control which files are indexed in settings.

data.title: First-time indexing
data.text: When you first open a large project, Cursor needs time to index it. You will see a progress indicator. Until indexing is complete, Cursor's codebase awareness will be limited. For very large repositories, consider excluding generated files and dependencies from the index in settings.

data.title: When to use each:
items: Use Chat for: understanding code, getting explanations, asking specific questions, generating single-file changes
Use Composer for: building new features across multiple files, large refactors, scaffolding projects, modifying architecture

data.title: Get the most out of Cursor:
items: Keep files small and focused — Cursor works better with smaller context windows
Use @-mentions to narrow context rather than pasting large files
Use the Tab key to accept inline suggestions; Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to accept Chat responses
Disable completions when you want to write freely without interruption
Use Composer's "Keep chat" option to maintain context across generations
